humanities_role_explanation: The benchmark explicitly targets domain-specific, graduate-level academic expertise across several humanities disciplines (e.g., Classics, Linguistics, History, Art History, Philosophy) rather than using humanities text merely as raw data for generic language tasks.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: The benchmark features multimodal questions comprising text-only items and items requiring the integration of text with an image reference (representing approximately 14% of the dataset).
analytical_tasks_explanation: The benchmark evaluates expert-level factual recall, multiple-choice QA, and exact-match short-answer QA across diverse subjects. It involves translation of ancient scripts (e.g., Palmyrene), logical and quantitative reasoning on world-class mathematics problems, cultural reasoning over local customs and historical trivia, visual recognition and reasoning over multimodal reference images, and testing calibration error to assess model uncertainty.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: HLE is a broad, multi-subject academic benchmark covering over a hundred subjects across STEM, humanities, and social sciences.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates several frontier LLMs including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, o1, DeepSeek-R1, and o3-mini.

quantitative_metrics.note: Evaluates models using accuracy and RMS calibration error.

published_after_march_2023.note: The paper is a preprint with a date of July 2026.

summary: This paper introduces Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a highly challenging multimodal benchmark consisting of 2,500 expert-written questions designed to test the absolute frontier of human knowledge across dozens of disciplines. By filtering out questions that current LLMs can easily answer, the benchmark provides a highly resistant test of expert academic capabilities, bridging mathematics, humanities, and sciences.
key_findings: State-of-the-art LLMs perform poorly on HLE, with the highest accuracy model (o3-mini) achieving only 13.4% accuracy. Furthermore, all evaluated models display high RMS calibration error (exceeding 70%), showing that they frequently generate incorrect answers with extremely high confidence.
review_notes: Both analysts had strong complementary readings. Reconciled analytical tasks by keeping well-supported labels from both sides: Cip correctly identified logical/quantitative reasoning and calibration tasks, while Ciop correctly identified cultural reasoning based on text evidence of 'local customs'. Selected 2026 for publication year based on the explicit date string in the arXiv preprint header. Consolidated the ASJC lists based on explicit mention of disciplines in the text.
facets_explanation: The reference answers were authored by nearly 1,000 recruited subject-matter experts to evaluate advanced academic reasoning and domain knowledge. Solving the questions requires retrieving specialized knowledge not contained within the question stimulus. The benchmark employs exact-match or multiple-choice questions with a single objectively correct answer. Divergent readings and peer-reviewer disagreements were treated as noise, resolved through an iterative review, rebuttal, and post-release audit process until consensus was reached.
results_explanation: The highest score reported on the benchmark is "13.4"% "Accuracy" by "O3-MINI (HIGH)*" on the text-only subset (Table 1). No human baseline solver score is reported, though the authors estimate an "expert disagreement rate of 15.4% for the public set" (Section B.3). Performance differences across answer formats (e.g. multiple-choice versus short-answer on identical items) or cultural groups are not evaluated or reported.
